title: Sanitization and Data Handling
subtopics: SQL and command injection prevention concepts
learning_outcomes: Explain how sanitization and data handling affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from validation versus sanitization to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on sanitization and data handling in validation, error handling, and api consistency. You will connect validation versus sanitization to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Sanitization and Data Handling matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying validation versus sanitization deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Validation errors, business conflicts, authentication failures, and unexpected server failures should be distinguishable and consistently represented. In this lesson, treat “Sanitization and Data Handling” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Sanitization and Data Handling
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.test/problems/validation",
  "title": "Request validation failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "One or more fields are invalid.",
  "errors": [{"field":"title","code":"required"}]
}
content_blocks.expected_output: The response uses an explicit, machine-readable validation error. The service should not include stack traces or secrets.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Validation versus sanitization”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Safe handling of user-provided strings” and “Preventing unsafe deserialization”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Distinguish client mistakes, business conflicts, and unexpected server failures. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating sanitization and data handling. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Validation versus sanitization” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Sanitization and Data Handling with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating sanitization and data handling as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Validation errors, business conflicts, authentication failures, and unexpected server failures should be distinguishable and consistently represented. In this lesson, treat “Sanitization and Data Handling” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
